stories.headline: 10-YEAR TREASURY YIELD TOUCHES 24-YEAR HIGH BEFORE PARING BACK TO 5.24%
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield spiked as high as 5.34% intraday Thursday — its highest level since 2002 — before easing 5 bps to close at 5.24% as traders took profits into the weekend. The move capped a seventh straight monthly climb, the longest streak since 2011, with the 30-year now above 5.68%.
stories.explain: Rising long-end yields reflect a higher term premium — compensation investors demand to hold duration — rather than a change in the Fed's policy rate itself, and here it's being driven by oil-led inflation fears and concern over heavy Treasury issuance funding the deficit. Because the 10-year anchors mortgage rates and corporate borrowing costs, financial conditions are tightening economy-wide even though Thursday's intraday pullback suggests some investors see the move as overextended.

stories.headline: FED'S SURPRISE HIKE TO 3.75%-4.00% NOW COLLIDES WITH A DATA BLACKOUT
stories.body: The FOMC voted 12-0 on Sept. 16 to lift the federal funds rate 25 bps to 3.75%-4.00%, its first hike in more than three years, wrong-footing markets that had been pricing cuts. With the federal shutdown now forcing the BLS to skip October's jobs report entirely, the Fed heads into its next meeting without the data releases it normally relies on.
stories.explain: A policy rate hike raises the risk-free rate used to discount every future cash flow, the direct channel compressing equity valuations and raising the bar for growth stocks to justify current multiples. The data blackout compounds that because the Fed can't confirm whether the labor market still justifies September's hawkish turn, so it will likely lean on noisier private substitutes like ADP payrolls and ISM surveys, which raises the odds of a policy misstep in either direction.

stories.headline: IRAN REJECTS CEASEFIRE TERMS, STRAIT OF HORMUZ STAYS SHUT AS CRUDE RALLIES
stories.body: The Trump administration rejected Iran's ceasefire conditions this week, prolonging the closure of the Strait of Hormuz — the chokepoint for roughly a fifth of global oil flows. Brent crude is now up about 42% from its late-June lows, and WTI touched $91.49 (+1.18%) Thursday with no formal talks scheduled.
stories.explain: Hormuz-transiting crude has no easy substitute route, so futures markets price in the probability-weighted risk of a prolonged disruption rather than waiting for an actual supply cut to materialize — which is why prices stay elevated even while oil is still technically flowing. Energy is a direct input into headline CPI and an indirect one into core goods via transport costs, making this the clearest channel tying the Hormuz standoff to the Fed's inflation calculus and this week's Treasury selloff.

stories.headline: SHUTDOWN BLACKS OUT OCTOBER JOBS REPORT, LEAVES FED 'FLYING BLIND'
stories.body: The Bureau of Labor Statistics confirmed it will not publish the October jobs report at all, with the November release pushed back to Dec. 16 — a near two-month gap in labor-market data. Federal employment alone is estimated to have fallen 162,000 in October, though furloughed workers who receive back pay are still counted as employed in the data that does exist.
stories.explain: Official labor and inflation data are the Fed's primary policy inputs, so a near-complete blackout forces reliance on higher-frequency but noisier proxies — ADP payrolls, job-postings trackers, the ISM services employment subindex — that track BLS prints imperfectly. Markets price in a wider range of outcomes when the Fed itself is uncertain, part of why Treasury volatility stayed elevated Thursday even as the headline yield level eased.

stories.headline: S&P 500 EDGES HIGHER, NASDAQ-100 SLIPS AS SMALL CAPS LEAD THE REBOUND
stories.body: The S&P 500 added 0.19% to 7,666.45 while the Nasdaq-100 slipped 0.16% to 30,359.21 as megacap tech lagged; the Russell 2000 jumped roughly 0.8% in afternoon trading, clawing back part of a rough September for small caps.
stories.explain: Small caps carry more floating-rate, shorter-duration debt, so they're more sensitive to the path of the Fed's policy rate and less to the 10-year's term-premium-driven climb, which is why they rebounded even as long yields stayed near 24-year highs. Megacap tech derives more of its valuation from cash flows far in the future, making it the more direct casualty of a higher discount rate even when the move is concentrated in the long end rather than the policy rate itself.

stories.headline: BIG EAST KICKS OFF 2026-27 SEASON AS FIRST POWER CONFERENCE TO HOLD MEDIA DAY
stories.body: The Big East hosted its Basketball Media Day at the Marriott Marquis in Times Square on Thursday, the first power conference to do so ahead of the 2026-27 season. The conference's 11 members open a preseason exhibition slate the first weekend of October as teams shift into full practice roughly five weeks from tip-off.

stories.headline: RAPTORS LOCK UP JAMAL SHEAD AS OCTOBER ROSTER DEADLINES LOOM LEAGUEWIDE
stories.body: Jamal Shead and the Toronto Raptors agreed to a three-year, $24 million extension tying the guard to the team through 2029-30. The deal comes as October brings a wave of roster and contract deadlines across the league, with several restricted free agents — including Detroit's Jalen Duren — still working through decisions as training camps open.

stories.headline: STEELERS SEND JOEY PORTER JR. TO COWBOYS FOR 2027 AND 2028 PICKS
stories.body: Pittsburgh traded cornerback Joey Porter Jr. to Dallas for a 2027 sixth-round pick and a 2028 second-round pick. The move came in a week otherwise dominated by injury news, with Vikings WR Justin Jefferson (ankle) sitting out Thursday's practice and Seahawks RB Zach Charbonnet opening his 21-day practice window as he nears a return from a torn ACL.

stories.headline: WEEK 5 HEADLINED BY NO. 7 ALABAMA AT NO. 16 MISSISSIPPI STATE, NOTRE DAME AT UNC
stories.body: College football's Week 5 slate spans Thursday through Saturday with 114 matchups across FBS and FCS. Saturday's headliners include No. 7 Alabama at No. 16 Mississippi State, No. 3 Notre Dame at North Carolina, and UCF at No. 20 Houston — a weekend several ranked teams face as their first real test of the season.

deepDive.title: Why an Oil Shock Can Move the Fed Even Without Jobs Data
content: Thursday tied together three threads that look separate but aren't: a 10-year Treasury yield that hit 5.34% intraday — a 24-year high — before settling at 5.24%; a Fed that hiked rates on Sept. 16 for the first time in three-plus years; and a government shutdown that just wiped October's jobs report off the calendar entirely. The common driver underneath all three is an energy-led inflation scare, with Brent crude up roughly 42% since late June as Iran keeps the Strait of Hormuz closed. Understanding how an oil shock moves a central bank that currently can't see official labor data is the single most useful mechanism in today's brief.

Oil feeds into inflation through two channels markets price differently. The direct channel is mechanical: gasoline and heating costs sit inside headline CPI, so a 42% crude rally shows up in next month's number almost automatically. The indirect channel is slower and more worrying to a central bank — transport and input costs filter into core goods prices over two to three quarters, and if the move lasts long enough, it can un-anchor the inflation expectations embedded in TIPS breakeven rates. It's that second channel, not the first month's headline print, that determines whether the Fed treats an oil shock as transitory or structural.

History's clearest parallel is 1973-74: an OPEC embargo quadrupled oil prices, and the Fed initially treated the shock as a one-off — a mistake that let inflation expectations de-anchor and ultimately forced the much harsher Volcker tightening cycle of the early 1980s. The lesson the Fed has internalized since is to watch inflation *expectations*, not just the current print, which is exactly the proxy problem today's shutdown creates: with CPI delayed and the jobs report skipped outright, the Fed is pushed toward higher-frequency stand-ins like the ISM prices-paid subindex and five-year breakeven rates, both of which tend to lead official CPI by several weeks but carry far more noise.

For a finance student, the practical takeaway is where to look next. With BLS data gated by the shutdown, the more informative numbers this month are ISM manufacturing and services prices-paid, weekly initial jobless claims (which keep publishing), and the 5-year TIPS breakeven — not the headline payrolls print everyone is used to watching. The 10-year's pullback off 5.34% Thursday hints the market may already see this oil shock as nearer the 1990 Gulf War case (a sharp, reversible spike) than the 1973 case (a durable regime change) — but that read will firm up only as the Hormuz standoff either resolves or drags into a second month.
